tracks.name: Querying Tables
tracks.description: Read rows, filter them, and summarise them with PostgreSQL.

lessons.title: 1. SELECT and FROM
lessons.summary: A query names the columns it wants and the table it reads from.

activities.title: Columns, then table
activities.instruction: `SELECT` lists the columns; `FROM` names the table. `*` means every column, which is convenient in the shell and rarely what you want in application code.

activities.title: Column order
activities.question: What order are columns returned in for `SELECT price, name FROM products`?
choices: The order they appear in the table
activities.explanation: The select list controls the output order. Rows without `ORDER BY` have no guaranteed order, but columns do.

activities.title: Read two columns
activities.instruction: Return the `name` and `price` of every product.

teaching.text: SQL reads like a sentence: select these columns from this table. The database returns a result set — rows of the columns you asked for.

SELECT name, price
FROM products;
Name the columns you use. `SELECT *` breaks quietly when someone adds a column, and it moves more data than the client needs.

lessons.task: Return the name and price of every product.
lessons.starterCode: -- Return the name and price of every product
hints: List `name, price` after `SELECT` and `products` after `FROM`.

SELECT name, price
FROM products;
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does `SELECT *` become a problem once a table has a large text or binary column?

lessons.title: 2. Filtering with WHERE
lessons.summary: WHERE keeps only the rows whose condition is true.

activities.title: One condition
activities.instruction: `WHERE` runs per row and keeps the ones that evaluate true. Combine conditions with `AND` and `OR`, and group them with parentheses when mixing the two.

activities.title: NULL comparisons
activities.question: How many rows does `WHERE discount = NULL` match?
choices: Every row where discount is empty
activities.explanation: Any comparison with NULL is unknown, so it never passes WHERE. Use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.

activities.title: Expensive products
activities.instruction: Return the `name` and `price` of products priced above 50.

teaching.text: Filtering in SQL happens in the database, close to the data. Pulling a whole table into JavaScript to filter it is slower and transfers far more.
Three-valued logic trips people up: `NULL = NULL` is unknown, not true. Always use `IS NULL`.

lessons.task: Return the name and price of products priced above 50.
hints: Add a `WHERE` clause after `FROM products`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is filtering in the query usually better than filtering the array in JavaScript afterwards?

lessons.title: 3. ORDER BY and LIMIT
lessons.summary: Sort the result and take just the first few rows.

activities.title: The three cheapest
activities.instruction: `ORDER BY column DESC` sorts descending. `LIMIT n` keeps the first n rows *after* sorting, which is what makes "top n" queries work.
activities.example:
SELECT name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price ASC
LIMIT 3;

activities.title: LIMIT without ORDER BY
activities.question: What does `SELECT * FROM products LIMIT 3` return without an ORDER BY?
choices: The three most recently inserted rows
Three arbitrary rows in no guaranteed order
activities.answer: Three arbitrary rows in no guaranteed order
activities.explanation: Without ORDER BY, row order is undefined. It may look stable in testing and change once the planner picks another plan.

activities.title: Top three
activities.instruction: Return the `name` and `price` of the three most expensive products.

teaching.text: `ORDER BY` sorts by one or more expressions. Add `NULLS LAST` when a nullable column should not lead the list.

SELECT name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 3;
For pagination use `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`. Past a few thousand rows, keyset pagination (`WHERE id > $1`) beats OFFSET.

lessons.task: Return the name and price of the three most expensive products.
hints: Sort descending on `price`, then keep three rows.

SELECT name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 3;
lessons.solution:
SELECT name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 3;
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why can paginating with a large OFFSET get slower as the page number grows?

lessons.title: 4. Counting and grouping
lessons.summary: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group; HAVING filters those groups.

activities.title: One row per category
activities.instruction: Every non-aggregated column in the select list must appear in `GROUP BY`. `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after.
activities.example:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
ORDER BY total DESC;

activities.title: WHERE or HAVING
activities.question: You want only categories with more than three products. Which clause takes `COUNT(*) > 3`?
activities.explanation: The count only exists after grouping, so it must be filtered with HAVING. WHERE cannot see aggregates.

activities.title: Busy categories
activities.instruction: Return each `category` and `COUNT(*)` as `total`, keeping only categories with more than 3 products.

teaching.text: Aggregates turn many rows into one: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`. Grouping decides what "one row" is grouped by.

SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
`COUNT(*)` counts rows. `COUNT(column)` skips NULLs in that column — the difference matters in reports.

lessons.task: Return each category with its product count, keeping categories with more than 3 products.
hints: Group by `category`, count the rows, then filter with `HAVING`.

SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
lessons.solution:
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM products
GROUP BY category
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why must every non-aggregated column in the select list appear in GROUP BY?

tracks.name: Relationships & Joins
tracks.description: Model related tables and combine them in one query.

lessons.title: 5. Primary and foreign keys
lessons.summary: Keys make relationships enforceable instead of hopeful.

activities.title: The database enforces the link
activities.instruction: A primary key uniquely identifies a row. A foreign key points at another table's primary key and makes the database reject rows that reference nothing.

activities.title: Orphan rows
activities.question: What happens when you insert an order with `customer_id = 999` that no customer has?
choices: It is stored with a null customer
The insert fails with a foreign-key violation
activities.answer: The insert fails with a foreign-key violation
activities.explanation: The foreign key is a constraint, not documentation. The database refuses rows whose reference does not exist.

activities.title: Create the orders table
activities.instruction: Create an `orders` table with an `id` primary key and a `customer_id` that references `customers(id)`.

teaching.text: Relational databases stay consistent because the schema states the rules: unique keys, required columns, valid references.
Decide what a deleted customer means for their orders. `ON DELETE CASCADE` deletes them; the default refuses the delete while orders exist.

lessons.task: Create an `orders` table with a primary key and a foreign key to customers.
hints: `id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY` gives each order an id.
customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id)
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What should happen to a customer's orders when the customer row is deleted?

lessons.title: 6. INNER JOIN
lessons.summary: Join keeps only the pairs where both sides match.

activities.title: Two tables, one result
activities.instruction: `JOIN` combines rows using the `ON` condition. An inner join drops rows with no match on either side.

activities.title: What gets dropped
activities.question: A customer has no orders. What does the inner join above return for that customer?
choices: A row with NULL order fields
Nothing — inner joins drop unmatched rows
activities.answer: Nothing — inner joins drop unmatched rows
activities.explanation: Inner joins only keep matched pairs. To keep customers without orders, use a LEFT JOIN from customers.

activities.title: Orders with customer email
activities.instruction: Return each order's `id`, `total`, and the customer's `email` by joining `orders` to `customers`.

teaching.text: The `ON` clause states how the two tables relate — almost always a foreign key to a primary key.
Qualify columns with the table name once more than one table is in play. `id` alone is ambiguous and the database will refuse it.

lessons.task: Return order id, total, and customer email with an inner join.
hints: Join `customers` and match its id to `orders.customer_id`.

FROM orders
INNER JOIN customers ON customers.id = orders.customer_id
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does an inner join make a customer with zero orders invisible in a report?

lessons.title: 7. LEFT JOIN
lessons.summary: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, matched or not.

activities.title: Find the customers with no orders
activities.instruction: With a left join, unmatched right-side columns come back NULL. Filtering `WHERE orders.id IS NULL` is the standard way to find missing relationships.
activities.example:
SELECT customers.email
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.id IS NULL;

activities.title: Filter placement
activities.question: Where must `orders.id IS NULL` go to keep unmatched customers?
choices: In the WHERE clause after the join
activities.answer: In the WHERE clause after the join
activities.explanation: A condition in `ON` only decides matching; it does not remove left-side rows. Filtering after the join is what selects the unmatched ones.

activities.title: Customers without orders
activities.instruction: Return the `email` of every customer who has no orders, using a LEFT JOIN.

teaching.text: Which table is "left" is decided by write order: `FROM customers LEFT JOIN orders` keeps all customers.

SELECT customers.email
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.id IS NULL;
For a count per customer, `COUNT(orders.id)` returns 0 for customers with no orders, while `COUNT(*)` wrongly returns 1.

lessons.task: Return the emails of customers with no orders.
hints: Left join orders onto customers, then keep the rows where the order side is NULL.

LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.id IS NULL
lessons.solution:
SELECT customers.email
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.id IS NULL;
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does COUNT(*) report 1 for a customer with no orders in a left join?

lessons.title: 8. Many-to-many joins
lessons.summary: Two joins bridge orders to the products inside them.

activities.title: Through the join table
activities.instruction: A junction table (`order_items`) holds one row per product in an order. Joining through it answers questions about both sides at once.
activities.example:
SELECT orders.id, SUM(order_items.quantity * products.price) AS total
FROM orders
JOIN order_items ON order_items.order_id = orders.id
JOIN products ON products.id = order_items.product_id
GROUP BY orders.id;

activities.title: Why store quantity
activities.question: Why does `order_items` need `quantity` instead of one row per item?
choices: So the same product can appear once with a count
activities.answer: So the same product can appear once with a count
activities.explanation: The pair (order_id, product_id) is unique, and quantity records how many. That also makes the composite primary key meaningful.

activities.title: Order totals
activities.instruction: Return each order `id` with its total value, joining `order_items` and `products` and summing quantity × price.

teaching.text: Many-to-many needs a third table. Each row in it is one pairing, often with extra columns such as quantity or price at purchase time.

SELECT orders.id, SUM(order_items.quantity * products.price) AS total
FROM orders
JOIN order_items ON order_items.order_id = orders.id
JOIN products ON products.id = order_items.product_id
GROUP BY orders.id;
Store the price paid on `order_items` if prices change. Recomputing historical totals from today's product price silently rewrites history.

lessons.task: Return each order id and its total value through the join table.
hints: Join orders → order_items → products, then sum quantity × price per order.
SUM(order_items.quantity * products.price) AS total
lessons.solution:
SELECT orders.id, SUM(order_items.quantity * products.price) AS total
FROM orders
JOIN order_items ON order_items.order_id = orders.id
JOIN products ON products.id = order_items.product_id
GROUP BY orders.id;
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is storing the price paid on the order line more reliable than joining to today's product price?

tracks.name: Changing Data Safely
tracks.description: Insert, update, and delete rows without losing the ones you meant to keep.

lessons.title: 9. INSERT
lessons.summary: Insert one row or many, and ask for the generated id back.

activities.title: Write a row and read its id
activities.instruction: `INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (...)` writes a row. `RETURNING` hands back generated values so you do not need a second query.

activities.title: String building
activities.question: Why build inserts with parameters (`VALUES ($1, $2)`) instead of template strings?
choices: Parameters prevent SQL injection and handle quoting
activities.answer: Parameters prevent SQL injection and handle quoting
activities.explanation: Values sent separately from the SQL are never parsed as code, so a name containing quotes — or an attack — stays data.

activities.title: Add a product
activities.instruction: Insert a product named 'Webcam' priced 35 in category 'video', returning its `id`.

teaching.text: Inserts list columns explicitly so the statement keeps working when the table gains a nullable column.
Multi-row insert: `VALUES (...), (...), (...)`. One statement for many rows is far faster than a loop of single inserts.

lessons.task: Insert a Webcam product at 35 in category video and return its id.
hints: Name the columns, then supply values in the same order.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is a single multi-row INSERT better than calling INSERT in a loop?

lessons.title: 10. UPDATE
lessons.summary: An UPDATE without WHERE rewrites every row in the table.

activities.title: Target one row
activities.instruction: `SET` lists the new values; `WHERE` chooses the rows. Check the row count before committing, and write the WHERE clause before you write SET.
activities.example:
UPDATE products
SET price = price * 0.9
WHERE id = 3
RETURNING id, price;

activities.title: Forgotten WHERE
activities.question: What does `UPDATE products SET price = 0` do with no WHERE clause?
activities.explanation: There is no implicit limit. The statement applies to every row in the table.

activities.title: Discount one product
activities.instruction: Set product 3's price to 90% of its current price and return the new `id` and `price`.

teaching.text: UPDATE is the highest-risk everyday statement. Always run the same WHERE in a SELECT first and count the rows.

UPDATE products
SET price = price * 0.9
WHERE id = 3
RETURNING id, price;
Wrap risky changes in `BEGIN;` … `COMMIT;` so you can `ROLLBACK;` after seeing the affected count.

lessons.task: Discount product 3 by 10% and return its new id and price.
hints: `SET price = price * 0.9` uses the old value while computing the new one.

UPDATE products
SET price = price * 0.9
WHERE id = 3
RETURNING id, price;
lessons.solution:
UPDATE products
SET price = price * 0.9
WHERE id = 3
RETURNING id, price;
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What is your routine for making a bulk UPDATE safe in production?

lessons.title: 11. DELETE
lessons.summary: Delete deliberately, and let foreign keys tell you what else depends on the row.

activities.title: Remove the cart's lines
activities.instruction: `DELETE FROM table WHERE ...` removes matching rows. `RETURNING` shows exactly what disappeared, which is the cheapest audit trail.

activities.title: TRUNCATE vs DELETE
activities.question: How does `TRUNCATE products` differ from `DELETE FROM products`?
choices: TRUNCATE removes all rows at once and cannot be filtered by WHERE
activities.answer: TRUNCATE removes all rows at once and cannot be filtered by WHERE
activities.explanation: TRUNCATE is a bulk operation that empties the table. DELETE can target rows and fire per-row triggers.

activities.title: Empty a cart
activities.instruction: Delete the rows in `cart_items` for `cart_id = 7`, returning the deleted `product_id` values.

teaching.text: Deletes are permanent unless you have a backup or a soft-delete column. Prefer `deleted_at` timestamps when users might need to undo.
A foreign key without `ON DELETE CASCADE` will block the delete while children exist — that is the constraint doing its job.

lessons.task: Delete cart 7's items and return the deleted product ids.
hints: Delete from `cart_items`, filtering on `cart_id`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When would a soft delete with a deleted_at column be a better choice than DELETE?

lessons.title: 12. Transactions and indexes
lessons.summary: Group changes so they all land or none do, and index the columns you filter on.

activities.title: All or nothing
activities.instruction: A transaction groups statements. `COMMIT` makes them permanent together; `ROLLBACK` discards them. Indexes make the lookups inside those statements fast.

activities.title: Half a transfer
activities.question: The second UPDATE fails inside a transaction. What is the state after `ROLLBACK`?
choices: Only the first update is saved
activities.explanation: The transaction rolls back as a unit. That is exactly why money transfers belong in one.

activities.title: Atomic transfer
activities.instruction: Move 100 from account 1 to account 2 inside a transaction, then add an index on `orders(customer_id)`.

teaching.text: Transactions protect invariants that span rows. Indexes protect response time: without one, a filter on a large table means a full scan.
Foreign keys do not index the child column automatically in PostgreSQL. Add the index yourself or every parent lookup scans.

lessons.task: Transfer 100 between two accounts in a transaction and index orders.customer_id.
lessons.starterCode: -- Move 100 from account 1 to account 2, then index orders
hints: Wrap both updates in `BEGIN;` … `COMMIT;`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a foreign key alone not make lookups on the child column fast?
